findings.statement: Broadcom's AI XPU platform comprises custom ASIC accelerators (AI XPUs) designed for AI inference workloads in data‑center and cloud environments. The company markets these AI XPUs as part of its AI infrastructure portfolio and has secured multi‑year orders for AI racks built around the XPU accelerators.

Broadcom delivers its AI capabilities through a subscription‑based licensing model via VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). VCF 9.0, released for FY 26, includes VMware Private AI Services as a standard component of the VCF subscription, removing the need for separate perpetual AI product licenses.

Broadcom’s AI infrastructure portfolio includes custom AI accelerators that are optimized for low power consumption and high performance, as well as merchant silicon connectivity solutions such as Ethernet and PCIe components. These hardware offerings are positioned for deployment in data‑center and cloud AI workloads, enabling large‑scale AI clusters.

Broadcom has an expanded partnership with Google Cloud that optimizes Broadcom’s VMware‑based AI solutions for Google Cloud and adds them to the Google Cloud Marketplace. The announcement is presented as a global initiative, indicating deployment of Broadcom AI computing solutions on Google Cloud in both the United States and Europe where Google Cloud operates.

Broadcom’s licensing model for AI‑related software (e.g., VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware Private AI Foundation) uses a subscription‑based approach with primary licenses for core platforms and add‑on licenses that provide additional capacity such as vSAN or AI foundation add‑ons. License capacity aggregates across active subscriptions, and usage analytics are available for customers to monitor consumption.

AMD Instinct GPUs are offered through several cloud service providers: Microsoft Azure (ND MI300X v5 instances) and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (BM.GPU.MI300X.8 bare‑metal) provide AMD Instinct at scale in both United States and European regions; IBM Cloud, Aligned, Cirrascale, TensorWave and Vultr also deliver AMD Instinct‑based instances globally. In Europe, Nscale operates a GPU cluster powered by Instinct MI250X accelerators in its Glomfjord data centre in Norway.

AMD’s AI‑focused hardware portfolio for cloud and data‑center workloads includes the Instinct MI455X and MI430X GPUs (part of the MI400 series), the Instinct MI350P PCIe accelerator cards, 6th‑generation EPYC™ server CPUs, the Helios AI rack‑scale solution, Ryzen™ AI Embedded X100 processors for edge/embedded AI, and the Kria™ AI System‑on‑Module and robotics developer platform.

AMD: Microsoft, a United States‑based cloud service provider, has deployed AMD Helios AI rack‑scale systems for its AI workloads. In Europe, the French sovereign‑cloud provider Scaleway has integrated AMD’s 5th‑generation EPYC server CPUs into its bare‑metal and AI service offerings.

Intel Corp: Intel’s AI compute portfolio for data‑center and cloud AI workloads includes its Xeon Scalable processors (including Xeon CPU Max), the Gaudi family of AI accelerators (Gaudi 2 and the newly announced Gaudi 3 PCIe card and 32‑node cluster), Intel Arc Pro GPUs and Data Center GPU Flex series. These products are positioned for both training and inference workloads and are integrated with Intel’s oneAPI and OpenVINO software stack to enable optimized performance. The Gaudi accelerators are offered in a standard PCIe Gen5 form factor and support Ethernet‑based scaling.

Intel Corp: Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers Intel‑based Habana Gaudi AI accelerators through its EC2 DL1 instance type, which is currently available in the United States East (Northern Virginia) and West (Oregon) regions and supports on‑demand, reserved, spot and savings‑plan pricing. IBM Cloud also provides access to Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators, extending Intel’s AI hardware presence in the cloud (regional coverage not specified). Intel’s partner listings confirm the AWS‑Gaudi integration for the Americas region.

Intel Corp: Intel’s AI hardware is monetized through cloud‑based usage models: AWS EC2 DL1 instances powered by Gaudi accelerators are sold on an on‑demand, reserved, spot or savings‑plan basis, providing flexible consumption pricing. Additionally, Intel’s AI software tools are offered under free‑license terms for a limited period, as described in its licensing FAQ.

Intel Corp: Intel currently offers a portfolio of AI compute products for cloud and data‑center workloads, including the 4th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors (available on AWS, GCP, Azure), the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series (up to 128 Xe cores, >500 TOPS), the Intel Data Center GPU Flex Series (Flex 140, Flex 170, Flex 170V with 16‑32 Xe cores and an industry‑first AV1 encoder), and a unified software stack via oneAPI toolkits (AI Analytics Toolkit, oneDNN, oneMKL, etc.) that enable optimized AI inference and training across CPUs and GPUs.

Intel Corp: Intel’s 4th Gen Xeon Scalable processors are offered as preview instances on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud Platform and Microsoft Azure, and are generally available on Alibaba Cloud; benchmark data show deployments on Azure US‑West and US‑East regions, confirming active use in United States data centers. Intel also partners with AWS, Cisco, Ericsson and Nokia to deliver private 5G solutions that incorporate Intel AI hardware, extending availability to Europe and the United States.

Intel Corp: Intel’s Data Center GPU Flex Series is sold under a recommended‑customer pricing model; Intel cites “up to 50 % lower total‑cost‑of‑ownership for VDI” as of 11 Oct 2023 compared with competing solutions. The oneAPI software toolkits are distributed under the Intel End User License Agreement (EULA) with component‑specific third‑party licenses, providing a royalty‑free, usage‑based licensing model for developers.

Broadcom sells its custom AI XPU ASICs as fully packaged chips directly to hyperscale cloud providers, indicating that the company not only designs but also delivers completed AI accelerator units to customers such as Google and AWS.
Broadcom reported AI semiconductor revenue of $10.8 billion in Q2 FY2026, a 143 % year‑over‑year increase, demonstrating a sizable revenue presence in the AI compute segment across its key markets.

AMD: The Instinct MI400 series, launched in 2026, includes the MI455X GPU for training and inference and the MI430X GPU for HPC. Both deliver up to 40 PFLOP (FP4) and 20 PFLOP (FP8) compute, feature HBM4 memory, and use the CDNA 5 architecture, representing a roughly two‑fold performance increase over the prior MI350 series.

AMD announced the Instinct MI500 series of AI accelerators, slated for launch in 2027. Built on the next‑generation CDNA 6 architecture, the MI500 GPUs will use a 2 nm process, HBM4E memory, and are projected to deliver up to a 1,000× performance uplift versus the MI300X GPUs introduced in 2023.

AMD unveiled the Helios rack‑scale AI platform, a turnkey solution that combines 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs with 18 sixth‑generation EPYC CPUs, integrated Pensando networking, and ROCm software, targeting yotta‑scale AI workloads in data centers.

AMD completed its acquisition of ZT Systems in March 2025 and announced the divestiture of ZT’s server‑manufacturing business for $3 billion, retaining ZT’s rack‑scale AI solutions design assets to accelerate AMD’s own AI infrastructure offerings.

AMD: At the Advancing AI 2026 event AMD introduced the 6th‑generation EPYC 9006 series server CPUs, marketed as the broadest portfolio for agentic AI workloads across cloud, enterprise, and HPC environments.
AMD: IDC’s AI Accelerator Vendor Share report for CY2Q25 shows AMD holding 1.8% of AI accelerator vendor revenue, placing it behind NVIDIA (85.2%) and Broadcom (10.3%).
AMD’s MI300 series GPUs, purpose‑built for AI training and inference, have attracted adoption by major cloud providers seeking alternatives to NVIDIA’s offerings.

Intel Corp: According to a Grand View Research report, Intel captured roughly 32% of the revenue share in the North American AI computer market in 2025, making it one of the leading vendors in the United States AI compute segment. The report does not provide a specific Europe share.
NVIDIA’s publicly documented AI offer areas include Accelerated compute, Data‑center systems, Networking and interconnect, AI software and developer tools, and Cloud access.
NVIDIA’s internal competitive assessment directs comparison of Broadcom alternatives on accelerator availability, interconnect, and system support.
U.S. market entry planning requires validation of existing and planned compute capacity, confirmed region/zone, capacity reservation, and service level.
European market planning mandates identification of the exact country and customer/use context and review of EU AI‑Act compliance.
CSP evaluation criteria highlighted by NVIDIA include available accelerator supply, qualified system configurations, deployment lead time, and serviceable capacity.
